title: Records issued in China: what to share with your GP in England
summary: For anyone bringing medical, prescription or vaccination records issued in China. What to show a GP in England, when translation may be needed, and how vaccination records are assessed.
content:
# Records issued in China: what to share with your GP in England

Last updated: 2026-11-27

> This guide covers **England**. Arrangements are different in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and we will cover them separately.

This Guide is about where the records were issued. Your nationality and the language you speak are separate. The linked GP registration and interpreting Guides apply to readers bringing records from elsewhere too. [Register with a GP](/en/health/registering-with-a-gp-england) · [Ask for an interpreter](/en/health/nhs-interpreter-language-help-england)

People who have been treated for years in China often arrive in the UK with a stack of medical record books, test results and discharge summaries, sometimes CT scans and their children's vaccination booklets too. Once here, the questions start: will a UK doctor want to see these? Do they need translating? Will everything have to be checked again from scratch?

For a UK GP to understand your medical history, you mainly rely on two things: the documents you bring, and what you explain clearly during the appointment. You don't need a lot of paperwork; what matters is picking out the useful parts so the GP can understand them.

## Register with a GP first, then explain your situation

If you have a long-term condition or take regular medicines, it is best to register with a GP practice soon after arriving in England, then book an appointment to tell the GP about the conditions you were diagnosed with in China, the medicines you take and any operations you have had. This is especially important if you have brought a limited supply of medicine: book before it runs out to leave enough time.

If your English is not good enough to explain your health clearly, you can ask for an interpreter when you book. Under NHS England guidance, interpreting for GP appointments should be free, and the practice should not ask you to bring your own interpreter. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-gp-interpreter-free)

To register with a GP, you are not required to provide identity documents or an NHS number; bringing medical records is to help the doctor understand you during appointments, and has nothing to do with registration. For how to register, see our separate guide on registering with a GP. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-registration-without-id-or-nhs-number)

## What to bring: more useful than a whole stack of records

We have not found any rule requiring you to give your GP all of your medical records from China. The list below is **what we suggest preparing**. It is not an NHS requirement, but with it your GP will understand your situation much faster:

- **diagnoses**: conditions you have had or are being treated for, and when they were diagnosed;
- **medicines you take now**: the generic name (the name of the active ingredient), not just the brand name; the strength in milligrams, how much you take each time and how many times a day; how long you have been taking it;
- **allergies**, and any reactions you have had to medicines or vaccines in the past;
- **operations and hospital stays**, with approximate dates;
- **recent test results**, such as blood tests and the written reports of scans;
- **specialist opinions or discharge summaries**, especially for conditions still followed up by a specialist;
- **vaccination records**, for adults and children.

Medicine names deserve a little more explanation. The NHS generally prescribes medicines by their generic name unless there is a clinical reason to prescribe by brand, so a UK doctor may not recognise a Chinese brand name; the name of the active ingredient is much clearer. It is usually on the box and the leaflet, so you can take photos before you leave, or ask your doctor in China to write it on your medicine list. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-generic-prescribing)

A simple summary of one or two pages, ideally with English, is much more practical than translating a whole record book. But be clear that this summary is reference information you put together yourself, not an official medical document.

## Do Chinese records need translating, and who translates them?

This needs to be stated precisely.

NHS England's guidance on translation for GP services includes these principles:

- health-related documents in other languages that patients bring when they register should, **where there is a clinical need**, be translated into English promptly, and where necessary both the original and the translation are kept in the record;
- documents translated for patients should be translated by competent, trained translators, **not by practice staff**;
- interpreting and translation services should be free at the point of use. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-translation-of-health-documents)

From these principles: not every page of your Chinese records needs translating; it depends on clinical need, and when translation is needed, a qualified translator should be used.

There are also some things for which we have not found a clear national rule:

- we have not found any rule requiring patients to get a certified translation first;
- we have not found a clear statement of who ultimately pays for translating records you bring yourself;
- we have not found official guidance saying machine translation or a family member's translation counts as a formal translation of medical records.

So a sensible approach is to prepare your own English summary to help communication and bring the Chinese originals as well. Which documents need formal translation, and how, depends on clinical need under the guidance; if you are unsure, ask the practice directly.

## Will UK doctors accept diagnoses and test results from China?

We have not found any rule requiring UK doctors to accept diagnoses or test results from abroad. Records from China are a valuable reference for your GP, but how they are used is up to the UK doctor's clinical judgement. They may use them directly, or decide that new tests or a fresh assessment are needed.

For scans (MRI, CT, ultrasound and so on), there are two separate things:

- **the written report**: the doctor's conclusions, which are easy to carry and to have translated;
- **the original images**: on a disc or as electronic files.

For scans brought from abroad, we have not found any national NHS England rule requiring hospitals to accept, import or use them. Each hospital handles them in its own way. There is no harm in bringing both the report and the images, but do not expect that this means tests will not be repeated in the UK.

## Continuing specialist care: usually through your GP first

If you have been seeing a specialist and having regular check-ups in China, in England you generally do not go directly to a hospital specialist for non-urgent care. You see a GP first, and the GP decides whether to refer you to hospital. NHS England's guidance to practices says GP referrals should be made on clinical grounds alone; whether care after referral is free is assessed separately by the receiving hospital. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-referral-on-clinical-grounds)

Letters and treatment plans from specialists abroad can help your GP understand your situation, but they do not mean you will definitely be referred, or that a UK specialist will continue the same treatment plan. When you are referred, in most cases you have the right to choose which hospital or service to go to. How long you wait depends on local circumstances. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-choice-of-hospital-on-referral)

## Vaccination records: bring them for adults and children

Vaccination records are a big concern for many families with children. In the UK, vaccination guidance comes from UKHSA (the UK Health Security Agency), and its guidance for health professionals is fairly clear:

- if there is a written record or a reliable verbal history, the record is used;
- **if there is no written record and no reliable verbal history, the person is generally treated as unvaccinated** and a full course of vaccinations is planned;
- people who had some vaccines abroad and then moved to the UK switch to the UK schedule and catch up according to their age;
- a course that has been started but not finished is simply continued; there is no need to start again. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-uncertain-immunisation-principles)

This guidance also applies to adults. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-immunisation-guidance-covers-adults)

Note that the vaccines used in China and the UK, and their timing, are not exactly the same. Which dose counts as which dose in the UK schedule is for health professionals to decide from the records, and we do not attempt a comparison here. What parents can do is bring their child's vaccination booklet, ideally with the vaccine name and date of each dose clearly visible, give it to the practice after registering with a GP, and ask what else the child needs.

The same goes for adults: if you have your own vaccination records, bring them and tell your GP.

## Allergies and past reactions

It is best to list medicine allergies, food allergies and any reactions you have had to injections or medicines separately, and to tell the doctor about them yourself during the appointment.

## How to prepare before coming to the UK or soon after arriving

- A one-page health summary in English: diagnoses, medicines you take (generic name, strength, dose, how often), allergies and reactions, operations;
- recent test reports and specialist opinions, with the originals;
- written reports of scans, plus the original images if you have them, but do not expect this to rule out repeat tests;
- vaccination records for adults and children;
- register with a GP as early as possible and, if you take regular medicines, book an appointment before they run out;
- if your English is not enough, ask for an interpreter when you book.

## Official sources

All of the sources below were accessed on 5 October 2026.

- NHS England — *You and your general practice* (Chinese version) — https://www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/you-and-your-general-practice-chinese/
- UK Health Security Agency (GOV.UK) — *Vaccination of individuals with uncertain or incomplete immunisation status* — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/vaccination-of-individuals-with-uncertain-or-incomplete-immunisation/vaccination-of-individuals-with-uncertain-or-incomplete-immunisation-status-from-1-july-2025
- UK Health Security Agency (GOV.UK) — *Vaccination of individuals with uncertain or incomplete immunisation status: supporting guidance* — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/vaccination-of-individuals-with-uncertain-or-incomplete-immunisation/vaccination-of-individuals-with-uncertain-or-incomplete-immunisation-status-supporting-guidance
- NHS England — *Primary medical services policy and guidance manual (PGM)*, Chapter 4 — https://www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/primary-medical-services-policy-and-guidance-manual-pgm-2/

- NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service — *Prescribing by generic or brand name in primary care* — https://www.sps.nhs.uk/articles/prescribing-by-generic-or-brand-name-in-primary-care/
